key_insight: Automated discovery harnesses are not universally superior; their apparent gains can come from specific design choices or random trial variance rather than a generally better framework. The paper argues that fair evaluation requires enough independent runs to separate real improvements from noise.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of comparing autonomous discovery systems when they are expensive, stochastic, and built from many intertwined components such as archives, selection rules, exploration strategies, and budget allocation. It highlights that too few trials can make weak harnesses look strong and strong ideas look insignificant.
method: Decompose discovery harnesses into their core design choices to evaluate which parts actually matter.
Compare harnesses across multiple independent trials to measure performance variability and reduce misleading conclusions.
Analyze how evaluation budget, stochasticity, and composite recipe design affect the reliability of claims about superiority.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work is a caution against trusting single-run or low-sample comparisons of autonomous discovery systems. It supports more rigorous benchmarking practices and can prevent wasted effort on methods that only seem better due to variance.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing harness components: archive, parent selection, exploration, and budget allocation.
A variance chart comparing performance across many trials versus a few trials.
A side-by-side benchmark graphic illustrating how different harness recipes can appear better under limited sampling.
An icon-based summary of stochasticity, cost, and evaluation budget.
paper_title: Automated Discovery Has No Universally Superior Harness
paper_authors: Akshat Gupta, Jermaine Lei, Alexander Lu, Gopala Anumanchipalli, Leshem Choshen
